oneSentence: A method that lets a model give different importance to different parts of the input while producing an output.
plainExplanation:
Imagine a model reading a sentence one token at a time. A token is a small unit such as a word or part of a word. Instead of treating every earlier token as equally useful, the model can compare the current token with the others and give more weight to the ones that seem more relevant.

What goes in are token representations, often called embeddings or vectors. A vector is a list of numbers that stores features in a form a model can calculate with. The attention mechanism uses these vectors to produce weights, sometimes called attention scores, that say how strongly one token should draw information from other tokens.

What happens next is not just selection but mixing. The model does not usually pick one earlier word and ignore the rest. It combines information from several tokens, but gives larger influence to some and smaller influence to others. That helps it connect words across a sentence, such as linking a pronoun to the noun it refers to.

What comes out is a new set of token representations enriched with context from elsewhere in the sequence. This is why attention became so important in transformers. It helps the model handle long-range relationships efficiently. Attention is a general mechanism, while self-attention is the specific case where the model attends to parts of the same sequence.

everydayAnalogy.title: Choosing the right notes during a meeting
everydayAnalogy.story: A project officer is writing a summary of a long meeting. For each sentence in the summary, she looks back at her notes and marks some lines as very useful, some as a little useful, and others as not useful for that sentence. She then writes the sentence using a blend of the most relevant notes rather than copying one line exactly. When she moves to the next sentence, she repeats the process with a different pattern of importance.

mapping.analogyElement: the sentence she is currently writing
mapping.aiElement: the current token position being updated or predicted

mapping.analogyElement: marking some notes as more useful than others

mapping.aiElement: combining information from multiple token representations

mapping.analogyElement: repeating with a new pattern for the next sentence

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A person may consciously understand the meeting and the purpose of the summary. An attention mechanism does not have that kind of human understanding. It performs numerical comparisons between vectors, and in many models this happens for all positions in parallel, not one handwritten sentence at a time.

visual.title: How attention shifts importance across a sentence
visual.learningObjective: After using this explainer, a reader should be able to say that attention lets one token gather more information from some tokens than from others, producing a context-aware representation.
visual.description: The explainer shows a short sentence as clickable tokens in one row and the currently selected token in a highlight box. Lines connect the selected token to all tokens, with thicker and darker lines for higher weights. A side panel shows weights as bars and a final mixed representation as a stacked bar.

steps.label: Choose a token
steps.explanation: The reader selects one token in the sentence to see which other tokens matter most for updating it.
steps.visualInstruction: Display 5 to 8 tokens in a horizontal row. Clicking a token adds a bold outline and updates all connections and bars.

steps.label: View importance
steps.explanation: Each connection shows relative importance, not a yes-or-no choice. Higher weight means greater influence on the selected token.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw SVG lines from the selected token to every token. Use line thickness and opacity to encode weight. Mirror the same values in a ranked bar list with numeric labels.

steps.label: See the mix
steps.explanation: The updated representation is formed by combining information from all tokens, with stronger contributions from higher-weight tokens.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a panel labelled 'mixed result' as a stacked horizontal bar or simplified vector strip. Colour segments by source token and scale segment width by weight.

steps.label: Try another focus
steps.explanation: When the reader selects a different token, the pattern changes. This shows that attention is recomputed for each position.
steps.visualInstruction: Allow the reader to click another token or use previous/next buttons. Update lines, bars and mixed result accordingly.

visual.interaction: Click or keyboard-select a token to change the focus; hover or focus on a bar or line to read its exact weight; use previous and next controls to step through the sentence.
visual.accessibilityDescription: Screen-reader version: 'Sentence: The committee approved the budget because it was urgent. Selected token: it. Relative weights from this token to others are listed from highest to lowest. approved: high. budget: medium. urgent: medium. the, committee, because, was: lower. The mechanism then forms a new representation for it by combining information from all tokens, with larger contributions from the higher-weight tokens. Selecting another token gives a different weighting pattern.'
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static version shows one selected token at a time with fixed connection lines and a ranked weight table beside it. Changing the token swaps the diagram instantly without animated movement or fading.

workedExample.scenario: A small language model is processing the sentence: 'Maria thanked Amina because she helped.' It needs a better representation for the token 'she'.
workedExample.input: Tokens: Maria | thanked | Amina | because | she | helped
process: The model compares the current token 'she' with the other tokens and calculates relative weights.
Suppose the weights come out like this: Maria 0.15, thanked 0.10, Amina 0.35, because 0.05, she 0.05, helped 0.30.
It then combines information from all token vectors using those weights, so Amina and helped contribute the most.
The new representation for 'she' now carries stronger context linking it to Amina and the action helped.
workedExample.result: The output is not a final answer by itself. It is a context-aware representation of 'she' that later parts of the model can use to predict the next token or analyse the sentence more accurately.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A country office uses an approved internal tool to help sort a shared inbox that receives messages about procurement, event invitations, travel requests and public information. When the system analyses a message, attention can help it focus more on terms such as dates, contract numbers or words that signal the topic.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This helps staff understand why a model may classify two similar-looking emails differently: it may be weighting different parts of each message.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place confidential, personal, protection-sensitive or security-sensitive email content into an unapproved public AI service. Human staff should review any automated triage before action is taken.

whyItMatters: If you use or oversee AI systems, attention helps explain why outputs change with context. That matters when judging reliability, debugging errors and deciding how much human review is needed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Attention means the model looks at only one word.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Usually it combines information from many tokens with different weights. The important idea is graded influence, not a single hard choice.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Attention shows what the model truly understood or why it answered.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Attention weights can be informative, but they are not a complete or universally accepted explanation of model behaviour. Other parts of the model also shape the output.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Attention and self-attention are the same term.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Attention is the broader mechanism. Self-attention is one case where tokens attend to other tokens in the same sequence.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is a way for a model to focus more on some parts of the text and less on others when updating each part.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Given token vectors, the mechanism computes relevance weights between positions and uses those weights to form weighted combinations of value vectors, producing context-dependent representations. In transformers, this is often implemented through query, key and value projections.

keyTakeaway: Attention helps a model use context by weighting which parts of the input matter most for each position.

quickCheck.question: What does attention mainly produce inside a transformer?
options: A weighted combination of information from different tokens
A permanent memory of all past training data
A grammar rule written by a human
A single correct explanation of the model's reasoning
quickCheck.explanation: Attention calculates relative weights and uses them to combine information from tokens. It does not create a human-written rule, store all training data for the task, or provide a complete explanation of model behaviour.
